questions.question: How much should we map before writing the standard down?

options.label: Cover the bad paths too (Recommended)
options.description: Map the normal case AND the three ways it currently goes wrong — bare list, jargon wall, buried in noise. Costs more discovery time, but those three failures are the whole reason the work exists, and a standard that only describes the good path can't be tested against them.

options.label: Just the normal path
options.description: Map only the straightforward case: a question is asked, you understand it, you answer. Faster to write. Risk: the standard describes what good looks like without pinning what bad looks like, so nothing catches a regression.

options.label: Go wide
options.description: Also research how other tools handle interrupting someone for a decision, and map several different kinds of asker. Thorough, but this is a prose standard for one plugin, and the extra breadth probably doesn't change what gets written.

options.label: A new person, defined here (Recommended)
options.description: Describe a new user: someone mid-task who gets interrupted by a question and has to reconstruct it before they can answer. Matches how every previous feature here was done, and this person's frustration genuinely isn't any existing one's.

options.label: Reuse an existing one
options.description: Attach this to one of the eight people already described. Cheaper, no new file. Risk: all eight of them hit this problem, so picking one implies the other seven don't.

options.label: Say it belongs to everyone
options.description: Treat it as applying to all eight existing users at once, with no new person. Honest about the reach. Risk: the traceability check wants a specific named person per piece of work, so this may just fail that check.

questions.question: Is 200 words a hard limit or a rough target?

options.label: Hard ceiling — a test can fail it (Recommended)
options.description: Over 200 words is a defect, countable and testable. Makes the standard enforceable rather than aspirational. Risk: an occasional genuinely complicated decision gets squeezed, so we'd need a stated escape hatch for where the extra detail goes.

options.label: Rough target, use judgement
options.description: Aim for about 200 words; going over is fine when warranted. Flexible and never squeezes a hard question. Risk: nothing can measure it, so it stays advice — which is the same category as the prose that already failed.

options.label: Hard ceiling on the question, detail allowed after
options.description: The ask itself must fit 200 words; unlimited supporting detail may follow, clearly separated, for when you want it. Testable and never squeezes. Risk: more moving parts, and the detail section could grow into the wall of text we're trying to kill.
